item.title: At the close: S&P 500 records best week since April 2025
item.description:
What a difference a week makes.

US equities capped a remarkable turnaround in holiday-shortened trading on Friday, with the major indexes building on Wednesday's gains as investors piled back into technology stocks.

Closing levels:

  • S&P 500 +1.39%

  • Nasdaq Composite +2.02%

  • DJIA +1.2%

  • Russell 2000 +1.5%

  • Toronto TSX Comp +1.2% (closes at the usual time)

The weekly gains were particularly impressive:

  • S&P 500 +5.6% — best week since April 2025

  • Nasdaq Composite +6.7% — best week since April 2026

  • DJIA +5.5%

There was some moderation in the gains from pre-market trading but the buying was widespread, with particular strength in the semiconductor and AI infrastructure names. Micron rose 8.7%, Dell gained 6.7%, AMD added 4.6% and Broadcom rose 3.8%.

Among the Magnificent Seven, Amazon led the way with a 4.0% gain, followed by Meta at 3.1%. Nvidia lagged with a gain of just 0.9% and that's one to keep a close eye on.

The rebound also extended to copper and other parts of the AI infrastructure trade, highlighting just how interconnected these trades have become. Freeport-McMoran was up 4.6%.

There are still plenty of questions about the economics of AI spending and how much infrastructure will ultimately be needed, but this week's price action suggests the market had gotten too pessimistic, too quickly. We saw that with the Fear & Greed Index bottomed this week at 9.

I wouldn't put too much weight on the moves in thin Black Friday trading in isolation, but the magnitude of the weekly gains is tough to ignore. The real test comes next week when liquidity returns and we turn the calendar to December, including next Friday's non-farm payrolls report.

Eyes will remain on Iran this week as the IRGC pledges to break the American shipping blockade. We heard today from CENTCOM that the US disabled a bulk carrier yesterday.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stock markets climb to the highs of the day as tech leads
item.description:
The S&P 500 is at the highs of today's holiday-shortened session.

Futures were strong ahead of the open but there was some immediate selling after the bell. That knocked the S&P 500 down to 7182 but it's since climbed to 7266, up 1.2% on the day. The Nasdaq is up 1.6%..

Among the winners are:

  • MU +5.6%
  • TSLA +4.7%
  • META +4.2%
  • AMZN +3.9%
  • AVGO +3.4%

The trouble spot is Nvidia, which is down 1.2% after opening higher. Keep an eye on that name. Microsoft and Google are also close to unchanged after strong opens. 

Zooming out, advancers lead decliners nearly 3:1 so there is plenty of sifting through the market to pick names. Outside the US, the Brazil EWZ ETF is up a whopping 10.4% after the selection of a market-friendly finance minister.

The latest investor sentiment numbers are also out from AAII and show both bearish and bullish views rising as neutral sentiment fell. That could reflect the intense volatility of November so far. That said, optimism about stock markets remains very high at 45.4% compared to its historical average of 31.5%

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: IRGC Navy commander says breaking the US naval blockade is imminent
item.description:
Iran's Revolutionary Guard is making huge amounts of noise today about breaking the US naval blockade.

The Commander of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard’s naval forces said zero hour for breaking the naval blockade is now imminent.  That was echoed by the aerospace force commander who said breaking the blockade is Iran's firm mission and unwavering determination. He also said the enemy should expect action in air and at sea.

I'm not sure why they would want to do this on a US weekend, as it works against the oil-price pain they have been leveraging but they have been talking about it for some time. The line has been that a status quo of neither war nor peace was intolerable. So they're escalating.

The oil market doesn't seem overly bothered here, with brent down $1.52 to $95.08. Perhaps this is seen as some kind of prelude to the endgame, as Congress looks to restrict Trump's ability to make war. Trump himself seemed to limit himself to striking something like Pickaxe mountain in his comments yesterday.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Brazil's EWZ up 13% as Lula hands the finance ministry to a banker
item.description:
Markets are pricing a Brazil without a fiscal crisis

The iShares MSCI Brazil ETF is up 13% in premarket trading after Lula named Bradesco chairman Luiz Carlos Trabuco Cappi as his finance minister for the term starting in January.

 After Lula's surprise win in October, USD/BRL rose above 6.00 and was there as recently as Monday. Equity markets craashed after the surprise election result. The worry was simple, Lula (in his fourth term) campaigned on an even-harder shift to the left with debt near 83% of GDP.

Instead, this is a major pivot that suggests the fiscal picture will remain credible and some of Lula's promises won't be met.

The moves:

  • USD/BRL is down nearly 4% today and touched 5.48. The pair opened the week at 5.95 and is on track for its biggest weekly fall of the year.
  • The Ibovespa rose 6.07% yesterday to 176,800 on reports that Trabuco had been sounded out. That was its best day since October, and futures are up another 2.85% today.
  • Long-dated swap rates are down more than 60 bps.

That's a powerful signal.

There's history here. In 2014 Dilma Rousseff reportedly offered Trabuco the same job. He turned it down and she went with Joaquim Levy, another Bradesco man. Levy lasted about a year before he was pushed out and replaced by Nelson Barbosa. So the market loves the name, but we will have to see how the marriage plays out.

Trabuco's job is a hard one. Analysts estimate the adjustment needed to get back to a primary surplus at more than R$80 billion. The PT's leadership in the lower house is already pushing back, and parts of the left say he's too market-friendly. Dario Durigan stays in the job until January and is already working on spending measures with Lula. Expect the first proposals to be judged against what the market now expects.

On the FX side, Brazil's carry is still among the best in the world, and the one thing holding the real back was fiscal credibility. Lula just bought some and there's a squeeze here as well with the market wrong-footed. But at 5.50 a lot of good news is priced in, and the real was at 4.88 in May before the election scare.

USD/BRL daily:

On the equity side, with the pre-market rally EWZ is trading at a trailing P/E of about 11.2x and a yield of 4.0%. Today's rally brings it back to virtually flat YTD.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: October US advance goods trade balance -149.5B vs -133.0B expected
item.description:
• Prior was -135.9B

That's going leave a dent in GDP forecasts.

Elsewhere:

  • Wholesale inventories +0.9% vs +0.8% prior
  • Retail inventories ex autos +0.6% vs +0.7% prior

The inventory data should somewhat offset the drag from trade.

For background, the advance international trade in goods report is published by the Census Bureau at 8:30 am ET as part of its Advance Economic Indicators release, roughly four weeks after the reference month ends. It's the earliest monthly read on US trade flows and lands alongside advance estimates for wholesale and retail inventories, making it a key input for GDP tracking.

The headline is the seasonally adjusted US goods trade deficit, the gap between the value of goods imported and exported. Both sides are broken down into six end-use categories: foods, feeds and beverages; industrial supplies and materials; capital goods; automotive vehicles, parts and engines; consumer goods; and other goods. The figures are in nominal dollars on a Census basis.

The advance report covers goods only. Services, where the US runs a surplus in areas such as travel, financial services and intellectual property, are added in the full international trade report from the Census Bureau and the Bureau of Economic Analysis about a week later. That report also revises the advance goods numbers and adds country-level detail.

For markets, the main relevance is GDP. Net exports are a component of growth, so a wider goods deficit generally subtracts from GDP and a narrower one adds to it. Paired with the inventory data released at the same time, the report frequently leads economists and nowcasting models such as the Atlanta Fed's GDPNow to revise their quarterly estimates.

Trade data have been unusually volatile. Surges in imports ahead of tariffs, followed by sharp pullbacks, have caused large swings in the deficit and in quarterly GDP. Big movements in nonmonetary gold, recorded under industrial supplies, have added noise, and economists often exclude gold to judge the underlying trend

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Green Friday: US stock futures surge as the AI trade comes back to life
item.description:
he rebound in US equity markets is picking up steam after the Thanksgiving holiday.

S&P 500 futures are up 1.7% while Nasdaq futures are up 2.4% as the technology rebound that started on Wednesday accelerates. US equity markets will close early today at 1 pm ET, so liquidity will be thin.

There is a strong bid across the Magnificent Seven in pre-market trading:

  • Meta +3.2%

  • Alphabet +2.6%

  • Amazon +2.6%

  • Nvidia +2.4%

  • Tesla +2.1%

  • Microsoft +1.9%

  • Apple +0.7%

The gains are even more impressive further down the AI food chain, with Bloom Energy up 7.5%, Nebius up 7.1% and Anthropic up 3.1%.

Copper is enjoying its biggest rally since January. Freeport-McMoRan is up 5.9% and Southern Copper is up 5.2%. The industrial metal has increasingly traded as a proxy for AI infrastructure spending given the amount of copper needed for data centres and associated power infrastructure. I disagree with that thesis but it's certainly been caught up in the termoil.

The big question for the broader market is whether this is the start of a sustained recovery or simply a squeeze after a bruising month for technology stocks. We saw a big rebound start on Wednesday after an early rout. I wouldn't read too much into price action in thin holiday trading, but the momentum from Wednesday is encouraging and there is some scope for month-end flows to add to the rally.

This has the potential to be the best week for the Dow Jones Industrial Average since April 2025.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: investingLive European session wrap: Post-Thanksgiving optimism lifts stocks, gold
item.description:
Headlines:

  • S&P 500 rebounds as growth concerns ease and Nvidia lifts sentiment, but underlying macro headwinds remain unchanged
  • Reminder: Wall Street is back today but will dip buyers have the last laugh?
  • Gold extends gains after a key technical breakout as broad short-covering improves sentiment
  • Gold begins to find its feet again but are buyers out of the woods yet?
  • How have interest rate expectations changed after this week's events?
  • France Q3 GDP revised lower as economic woes deepen
  • France inflation undershoots estimates in November as energy and services price pressures ease
  • Spanish inflation comes off the boil in November, offering some respite for the ECB
  • Germany unemployment rises more than expected in November as labour market struggles persist

Markets:

  • AUD leads, JPY lags on the day
  • 10-year Treasury yields up 5 bps to 4.897%
  • Gold up 2.9% to $3,668
  • Bitcoin up 1.2% to $61,479
  • European equities modestly higher; S&P 500 futures +1.6%

It looks like US traders are returning from their Thanksgiving dinner with renewed appetite for risk as well, with US futures rallying ahead of the return of Wall Street later.

Tech shares are leading the charge as investors look to build on Wednesday's turnaround, with S&P 500 futures up by 1.6% and Nasdaq futures up by 2.1% currently. European equities are also joining in on the fun, albeit with considerably more modest gains.

Gold is a standout mover with the precious metal up nearly 3% on the day to $3,668 as the rebound continues. Meanwhile, the dollar is keeping more mixed as it holds its own against the euro and yen but is down against the aussie amid the better risk mood. At the same time though, Treasury yields are nudging up again with 10-year yields up close to 5 bps to near 4.90%.

Typically, higher bond yields make life a little more difficult for both gold and richly valued tech stocks. Yet, both are enjoying quite the rebound today.

That doesn't necessarily mean that something is amiss though. After the beatdown that both have endured this month, some of the buying here could simply be traders unwinding bearish bets rather than investors suddenly turning bullish again. So, there's that to consider.

And that is not to mention that today's trading conditions will offer much clarity either. US markets are back open for an abbreviated session but plenty of traders are likely still enjoying an extended Thanksgiving break. As such, even relatively modest orders can end up moving prices quite considerably amid thinner liquidity conditions.

Then, there's also potential month-end portfolio rebalancing in play and it becomes even harder to separate genuine shifts in market sentiment from money being moved around for largely mechanical reasons.

But for now though, we're definitely seeing dip buyers and the optimists find themselves some much needed breathing room. At this juncture, there's certainly the temptation to buy the dip. However, let's be reminded that there's a difference between markets finding a bit of relief and traders finding their conviction again.

There are definitely signs of the latter, more so than earlier in the week, but the blurry trading conditions today will make it hard to tell for sure if we're truly back with a bang. I reckon we'll only get a better sense of that come next week.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Black Friday's Record Spending Trap: Why Good Economic News Isn't Always Good Market News
item.description:
Black Friday could deliver another record-breaking day for US consumer spending, with unprecedented retail sales painting a picture of remarkable consumer resilience.

And yet financial markets could still respond negatively.

That is not a contradiction. It reflects one of the most important distinctions in trading: the difference between good news and news that is better than expected.

Financial markets are forward-looking. By the time Black Friday spending figures arrive, investors have already formed expectations about consumer demand, corporate earnings, inflation and monetary policy.

Against the backdrop of a technology-led equity market correction and renewed questions over AI valuations, consumer resilience could offer investors a reason to look elsewhere for earnings growth.

But the significance of Black Friday lies less in whether records are broken and more in whether the assumptions underpinning current asset valuations are challenged.

A Record Is Not Necessarily a Positive Surprise

Adobe Analytics forecasts US online holiday spending of $275.1 billion in 2026, an increase of 6.7% year on year. Black Friday itself is expected to generate $12.9 billion, with Cyber Monday projected to reach $15.1 billion.

The expectation is already one of record spending.

Source: Adobe Analytics, 2026 US Holiday Shopping Forecast.

Consider a hypothetical scenario in which Black Friday online spending reaches $12.5 billion. It would represent a new record and approximately 6% annual growth, yet fall short of Adobe's forecast.

The same data point can simultaneously confirm growth and disappoint expectations.

A strong number that confirms existing expectations may have limited implications for valuations. A weaker number that exceeds pessimistic expectations can produce a more significant positive response.

While published forecasts do not necessarily reflect exactly what markets have priced in, the principle remains important. When assessing Black Friday's impact on financial markets, traders should be asking not simply whether spending increased, but whether it materially changes existing expectations.

More Spending Does Not Necessarily Mean More Consumption

Headline retail sales figures measure expenditure rather than the quantity of goods and services consumers purchase.

In an inflationary environment, households can spend more without consuming more. Higher expenditure may reflect rising prices rather than stronger purchasing power.

For an economy in which household consumption accounts for approximately two-thirds of economic activity, the quality of spending growth matters as much as its magnitude.

Source: Mastercard Economics Institute and SpendingPulse, 2026 Holiday Forecast.

The composition of expenditure offers another layer of insight. Adobe forecasts online grocery spending growth of 10.3% over the holiday season, compared with 5.9% for electronics and 4.7% for apparel.

Source: Adobe Analytics, 2026 US Holiday Shopping Forecast. Figures represent forecast year-on-year growth in nominal online expenditure.

Stronger growth in essential categories could indicate that consumers are using seasonal discounts to reduce everyday costs rather than expand discretionary expenditure.

Differences in pricing and the migration towards online shopping could also explain these trends. Nevertheless, spending driven by necessity tells investors something very different from spending supported by rising real incomes and discretionary purchasing power.

Demand Today. At the Expense of Tomorrow?

Black Friday introduces another complication: the timing of consumption.

A household intending to purchase a television in December may bring that purchase forward to November to secure a discount. November spending increases, but total consumption across both months remains unchanged.

Economists refer to the allocation of consumption across different periods as intertemporal substitution.

Buy now, pay later services add another dimension, supporting immediate purchasing activity while distributing financial obligations across subsequent months.

While this does not necessarily indicate financial distress, the sustainability of spending depends partly on whether it is supported by income growth, savings or future financial commitments.

A strong November followed by weaker December or January expenditure could challenge the initial narrative of consumer resilience.

The question is whether Black Friday is generating additional demand or simply redistributing it.

Record Sales. But What Happens to Earnings?

Revenue growth is not synonymous with earnings growth.

Retailers competing aggressively for holiday spending may generate higher sales through deeper discounts and greater promotional expenditure, potentially placing pressure on profitability.

Consider a simplified hypothetical example.

Illustrative figures only. The example does not represent actual corporate performance or industry benchmarks.

The retailer generates record revenue, yet earns less gross profit.

Promotional intensity, inventory management, operating costs and subsequent earnings guidance can therefore be more revealing than headline sales growth.

For investors, the important question is not simply how much demand a retailer captured, but how economically it captured that demand.

Can the US Consumer Give Wall Street a Reason to Look Beyond AI?

The recent technology-led equity market correction has raised questions about valuations, capital expenditure and the timing of returns on AI infrastructure investment.

When confidence in the companies that have dominated major capitalisation-weighted indices weakens, the ability of other sectors to support market performance becomes increasingly important.

Resilient consumer demand could provide an alternative source of earnings growth across retailers, consumer discretionary businesses and other consumer-facing companies.

The opportunity is not for Black Friday to reverse the correction, but for evidence of economic resilience to help broaden the foundations of a potential recovery.

This is where market breadth becomes particularly relevant.

An S&P 500 recovery driven by a handful of technology stocks tells investors something different from an advance supported by multiple sectors.

Comparing equal-weighted and capitalisation-weighted indices, monitoring relative sector performance and assessing earnings revisions can help traders distinguish between the two.

A strong consumer cannot resolve concerns over AI investment returns. It could, however, reduce the market's dependence on a single growth narrative.

When Good Economic News Becomes Bad Market News

Equity valuations are influenced by expectations for future corporate cash flows and the discount rate applied to those cash flows.

Stronger consumer demand can improve the first while placing upward pressure on the second.

If subsequent economic releases confirm resilient consumption alongside persistent inflation, investors could reassess the scope for monetary policy easing.

Higher expected interest rates can support bond yields and place pressure on equity valuations, particularly for growth companies whose expected earnings are concentrated further into the future.

Resilient demand and persistent inflation could also support the US dollar, while higher real yields and a stronger dollar could create headwinds for gold.

Conversely, weaker consumption could support expectations of monetary easing while raising concerns about corporate earnings.

Neither outcome is universally positive. The market reaction depends on which component of asset valuation investors are most concerned about.

Importantly, preliminary Black Friday figures are unlikely to materially alter Federal Reserve policy expectations on their own. Subsequent official retail sales, personal consumption expenditure and inflation data will provide a more substantial basis for reassessment.

The Holiday Liquidity Trap

The shortened US equity trading session on Black Friday and potentially lower market participation over Thanksgiving can reduce market depth, allowing relatively modest order imbalances to generate disproportionately large price movements.

Cyber Monday also coincides with the final trading day of November in 2026, introducing potential month-end rebalancing flows unrelated to consumer spending.

The shortened US equity trading session on Black Friday and potentially lower market participation over Thanksgiving can reduce market depth, allowing relatively modest order imbalances to generate disproportionately large price movements.

Cyber Monday also coincides with the final trading day of November in 2026, introducing potential month-end rebalancing flows unrelated to consumer spending.

At EC Markets, we see the ability to distinguish between changes in market fundamentals and changes in market conditions as central to informed trading decisions.

A large price movement does not necessarily represent a large change in fundamental value

Bottom Line

Black Friday offers an opportunity to reassess US consumer resilience at a time when investors are questioning the sustainability of technology-led equity market growth.

But record spending, stronger corporate earnings and improved asset valuations are three distinct outcomes. One does not automatically lead to the next.

The task for traders is to understand not only what the data says, but what it changes about the assumptions already reflected in market prices.

Consumers spend Black Friday looking for value. Traders should be doing the same.

Because financial markets do not simply reward good news. They reward developments that improve upon what was already expected.

 

This article was written by IL Contributors at investinglive.com.

item.title: S&P 500 rebounds as growth concerns ease and Nvidia lifts sentiment, but underlying macro headwinds remain unchanged
item.description:
The S&P 500 rebounded this week as growth concerns peaked in the near-term and the news of Jensen Huang being reinstated as Nvidia CEO following pressure from the White House improved the risk sentiment. The recent rally fuelled hopes that the recent stock market selloff could be coming to an end.

The argument for the S&P 500 to recover all the losses and eventually reach new record highs is based on the idea that the weakness was largely driven by Nvidia's troubles and concerns about the AI boom. Moreover, the White House's intervention implicitly signalled that the administration will do everything in its power to keep the AI investment cycle going.

I'm sympathetic to this view, but the selloff wasn't driven by Nvidia alone. Credit spreads had already been widening well before Huang's scandal, reflecting growing concerns about the economic outlook amid a more hawkish Fed and prolonged US-Iran tensions. Neither of these two major drivers has changed.

The dovish repricing we've seen in recent weeks has largely been driven by the stock market selloff itself, which exacerbated growth concerns and dragged down many commodities. It wasn't the result of a meaningful improvement in the inflation outlook. Therefore, if equities recover, upside inflation risks will persist, potentially giving the Fed even more confidence to continue tightening monetary policy.

For now, the lack of fresh bearish catalysts and the more positive sentiment is keeping the stock market afloat, but the outlook remains neutral to bearish. A sustainable bullish reversal would likely require either a more dovish Fed or a breakthrough in the US-Iran situation as it would remove a major source of uncertainty and improve the global growth outlook.

 

S&P 500 TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that the S&P 500(CFD contract) is trading at the resistance zone around the 7,300 level. We can expect the sellers to step in around the resistance, with a defined risk above it, to position for a drop into the 6,300 level. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to extend the rebound into the downward trendline.

S&P 500 TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 4 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 4 hour chart, we have an upward trendline that could act as support in case the price pulls back. We can expect the buyers to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk below it, to keep targeting new highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking lower to increase the bearish bets into new lows.

S&P 500 TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – 1 HOUR TIMEFRAME

On the 1 hour chart, we have a minor upward trendline defining the bullish momentum on this timeframe. The buyers will likely continue to lean on the trendline, with a defined risk below it, to keep pushing into new highs. The sellers, on the other hand, will look for a break lower to increase the bearish bets into the next trendline around the 7,050 level. The red lines define the average daily range for today.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

Interest rate expectations remained largely unchanged this week given the lack of major macro or geopolitical developments. The prolonged US-Iran stalemate, growth concerns and persistent inflation risks continue to shape the outlook. The more notable moves came from Canada and Australia, where central bank commentary and economic data led to some changes in interest rate expectations.

The Bank of Canada saw the most notable hawkish repricing. Hawkish remarks from BoC members this week reinforced expectations of another rate hike coming in December and potentially more in 2027. I think the BoC is making a policy mistake given subdued inflationary pressures, soft labour market and negative growth drivers.

On the RBA side, we've got some more dovish repricing despite hotter-than-expected inflation data this week. The market is looking beyond the near-term conditions and placing greater weight on weakening economic activity confirmed by the softer PMIs on Monday and the deteriorating labour market conditions.

Elsewhere, expectations remained relatively unchanged. Looking ahead, the focus will be on the key US data coming in the next two weeks and of course the December FOMC meeting which could deliver a hawkish surprise.

item.title: Solana remains mostly rangebound as the negative macro backdrop limits the recovery. What's next?
item.description:
Solana has been consolidating near recent lows as the crypto market remains under pressure from tightening financial conditions. There has been some broad short-covering, but no positive catalyst backing the move.

Keep in mind that cryptocurrencies are very sensitive to changes in liquidity and risk sentiment, so higher interest rates and tighter financial conditions tend to be strong bearish drivers.

In terms of macro fundamentals, the picture remains largely unchanged. The Fed is still expected to raise rates, with the extent of tightening depending on incoming economic data and stock market conditions. The prolonged US-Iran stalemate is another source of uncertainty, keeping energy prices and inflation risks elevated while weighing on future growth expectations.

On the Solana-specific front, there haven’t been major developments after the network completed the Alpenglow consensus upgrade in October.

Looking ahead, the upside in Solana will likely remain limited as long as macro conditions remain unfavourable. A sustained recovery will likely require a more dovish Fed or a breakthrough in the US-Iran situation as would improve global growth expectations.

 

SOLANA TECHNICAL ANALYSIS – DAILY TIMEFRAME

On the daily chart, we can see that Solanahas been consolidating around recent lows. If we get a pullback into the major downward trendline, we can expect the sellers to lean on it, with a defined risk above it, to keep targeting the 60.00 level. The buyers, on the other hand, will want to see the price breaking higher to pile in for a rally into the 98.00 level next.

item.title: Connecting the dots: When does the AI selloff become a Fed problem?
item.description:
At what point does Nvidia's falling share price become the Fed's headache?

Now, wait a second. That sounds a little silly, doesn't it? But given how much of the US economic growth story is riding on AI these days, I wouldn't laugh off that question so easily.

Let's say you have made a decent amount of money from the stock market over the past few years. You're feeling a little richer and perhaps more comfortable about booking that family holiday or even splurging on a new car. But out of nowhere, a good chunk of those gains disappears in just a matter of weeks. Suddenly, that old car doesn't look so bad after all now, does it?

Economists call this the wealth effect. And you don't necessarily have to sell your stocks to change your spending habits. Just the notion of feeling poorer can be enough. And while stock market wealth is largely concentrated among the richer households, a prolonged selloff could still take some of the shine off US consumer spending as a whole.

This is where the AI boom also puts food on a lot more tables than we might realise.

Take for example building a data centre. It isn't just about buying a truckload of Nvidia chips. You need construction workers, electricians, cooling equipment, power supplies and plenty of other things. Just think that there are entire businesses banking on the assumption that the tech giants will keep spending as aggressively as they have been.

Now, a falling share price alone probably won't persuade Microsoft or Amazon to abandon their AI ambitions. But if those investments aren't making as much money as promised, shareholders might become a little less forgiving. And not everyone in the AI business has deep pockets. It's one thing to build a data centre with money you've already earned, but it's a whole other thing to borrow millions today on the assumption that you'll make enough money from AI tomorrow. So if lenders start questioning those assumptions, they might demand higher interest rates or become less willing to lend altogether.

All of a sudden, a data centre project that made perfect financial sense six months ago might no longer be worth pursuing. And the Fed wouldn't have needed to raise interest rates by a single basis point for that to happen.

In continuing to see how all of this is trickling down, fewer projects mean fewer orders. And that means a supplier might hold off hiring more workers, while a contractor might find itself having to let some people go.

In turn, those workers might spend less at restaurants, shops and other businesses that have absolutely nothing to do with AI. In essence, nobody needs to lose their life savings for an AI bust to hurt the economy.

Can you see where all of this is going now?

Typically, weaker consumer spending and a softer jobs market would strengthen the case for the Fed to lower interest rates. However, we are being caught in a higher for longer backdrop now with inflation pressures looking quite unforgiving. And that is even discounting the fact that the AI productivity miracle that was supposed to help businesses produce more at a lower cost looks to be taking longer to materialise.

As such, we could end up with weaker economic growth without quite the same relief on inflation. And that would leave policymakers at the Fed in a rather uncomfortable spot.

The Fed doesn't have a mandate to protect your stock portfolio. It does, however, have one to support employment and maintain price stability. And that's why traders should not only be concerned about how much further tech stocks might fall. They should really be worried about how much of the economy might get dragged down with tech stocks if the selling continues.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

On the news front, Trump touted the US naval blockade and continued military deployment while saying that Washington is still giving Iran an opportunity to reach an agreement. He also threatened to strike Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain if no deal is reached.

Overall, there’s been no de-escalation nor improvement in the US-Iran situation as the risk of a direct military confrontation remains high. In terms of fundamentals, the macro picture remains largely unchanged. The Fed is still expected to raise rates, with the extent of tightening depending on incoming economic data and stock market conditions. The prolonged US-Iran stalemate is another source of uncertainty, keeping energy prices and inflation risks high while weighing on future growth expectations.

Looking ahead, the upside will likely remain limited for Ethereum as long as financial conditions stay tight and risk sentiment remains cautious. A sustained reversal will likely need a more dovish Fed or a breakthrough in the US-Iran situation as that would improve future growth expectations.

item.title: Germany unemployment rises more than expected in November as labour market struggles persist
item.description:
• Germany November unemployment change 9k vs 4k expected
  • Prior 4k
  • Germany November unemployment rate 6.4% vs 6.4% expected
  • Prior 6.4%

The number of people out of work in Germany rose by more than expected in November, though the jobless rate is seen holding steady on the month at 6.4%. Overall, the total number of unemployed persons rose to 3.025 million in seasonally adjusted terms.

But when looking at the unadjusted total, it fell by 19,000 to 2.936 million in November with the labour office noting that the decline reflected the end of the autumn seasonal pickup. However, I'd put more weight on the seasonally adjusted figures here as they strip out the usual seasonal fluctuations and offer a better indication of the underlying health of the labour market.

As for the overall report, the labour office noted that "the trend of recent months is continuing" and that "the slight economic recovery has not led to revival in the labour market in November".

If you couple that with the subdued consumer confidence figures yesterday, then you can see why there are still concerns about the sustainability of the recovery. If households become more worried about job security, they're more likely to hold back on spending. That will then give businesses even less incentive to expand and hire.

In turn, it also makes life more complicated for the ECB, which is still having to contend with elevated inflation despite pockets of economic weakness across the region.

Looking to next year, I'd keep a close eye on whether the weakness in hiring starts to translate into more widespread job cuts. A more sluggish labour market is one thing but a more pronounced deterioration in employment could make Germany's economic recovery considerably harder to sustain.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

Looking ahead, gold will likely need support from a dovish repricing in interest rate expectations either from weaker data, dovish Fed commentary or an end to the Iran war. item.title: Spanish inflation comes off the boil in November, offering some respite for the ECB
item.description:
• Spain November preliminary CPI +4.1% vs +4.6% y/y expected
  • Prior +4.9%
  • Spain November preliminary HICP +4.1% vs +4.7% y/y expected
  • Prior +4.9%

Much like the French report earlier, Spain's inflation numbers are also seen cooling off in November. After nearly hitting 5% in October, headline annual inflation is seen dropping back to 4.1% this month. The added good news is that core annual inflation was also estimated to drop to 2.6% in November, as compared to the 3.1% reading in the month before.

That being said, these figures are all still too high for any comfort for the ECB. And that's the troubling part for the central bank as they are dealing with quite an array of inflation backdrops across the region at this stage.

But as a whole, policymakers are arguably very much concerned about the risks of potential second-round effects. So, that remains the priority in terms of policy setting.

As things stand, they are likely to be able to get away with another rate hike in December. And the market pricing reflects roughly 93% odds of a 25 bps move already. But in looking to next year, the challenge will be how the central bank balances any further tightening measures against slowing economic growth.

The fiscal risks from France and now more trouble from US tariffs will make things even more challenging for the ECB. So, therein lies their predicament as we move to the final stages of the year.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: France inflation undershoots estimates in November as energy and services price pressures ease
item.description:
• France November preliminary CPI +2.9% vs +3.2% y/y expected
  • Prior +3.4%
  • France November preliminary HICP +3.2% vs +3.6% y/y expected
  • Prior +3.7%

Well, that's some good news for the French economy as inflation pressures are seen cooling back a little in November. The drop here is even below analyst estimates, with headline annual inflation dropping back below 3%. The monthly reading also shows that French inflation should ease by 0.7% in November, after having risen by 0.4% in October.

Looking at the details, energy inflation falling off is a key factor driving that development. Of note, energy prices are seen rising by 19.2% in November compared to the 24.1% increase in October.

That being said, core prices are also likely to come off the boil as services inflation cooled as well. Services prices were seen down to 2.3% in November compared to 2.6% in the month before.

All in all, the ECB can take some comfort in that as this will reduce stagflationary risks in Europe's second-largest economy. But even then, price pressures are admittedly still on the higher side and policymakers cannot rest on their laurels just yet.

For now, all of this still supports the argument that they may perhaps get away with another rate hike. But after, they will have to seriously consider the balance of risks between overtightening monetary policy and the necessity to tame the inflation monster amid potential second-round effects.

In other words, they will still be in a tough spot in trying to decide on policy so as to risk sending the economy off the ledge or allowing inflation pressures to grow to be too overwhelming. That will be the key challenge for policymakers next year.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: France Q3 GDP revised lower as economic woes deepen
item.description:
• France Q3 final GDP -0.2% vs -0.1% q/q prelim
  • Prior 0.0%

Ouch. France was already the troubling spot in the euro area and the negative revision to the preliminary GDP estimates only continues to underscore that notion. In volume terms, the French economy contracted by 0.2% in Q3 following some tentative stability in the previous quarter.

Domestic demand was pretty much subdued, stagnating on the quarter, while inventory changes contributed to 0.3% to quarterly GDP with net foreign trade being the main drag with a negative contribution of 0.6% on the quarter.

Overall, the French economy is seen growing by just 0.1% so far this year and that is hardly encouraging for Europe's second-largest economy.

As such, this won't steer the conversation away from stagflationary risks as we head into next year. The only good news is that the latest French inflation numbers for November is at least showing some signs of cooling, affording the ECB some added breathing room in looking to the French economy as a whole.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: US reportedly urged Venezuela, Iraq to consider quitting OPEC earlier this year
item.description:
US president Trump has never been much of a fan of OPEC. And as it would seem, he'd quite like a few of its members to feel the same way.

In an exclusive report by Reuters today, the US administration is said to have encouraged Venezuela and Iraq to contemplate leaving OPEC earlier this year. Washington reportedly even blocked Venezuela's annual membership payment, while Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman intervened over the summer to persuade the US to back off.

Despite such actions, the US State Department has maintained that an OPEC exit was not raised at senior levels with Venezuela and that discussions with Iraq centred on energy infrastructure. Sure, sure.

Now, this is all very on brand for Trump given his longstanding disdain for OPEC and the bloc's influence over oil prices. However, there is also arguably a commercial angle here. If Washington wants US oil companies to ramp up production in both countries, why have a third party dictating how much oil they can pump out of the ground?

Having said all that, the political realities are a little more complicated though.

For Venezuela, which is currently exempt from OPEC production quotas, walking away offers little to no immediate benefit. They would essentially be giving up its seat at the table before their oil industry has even fully recovered.

Meanwhile, Iraq's oil ministry has maintained that their position is more in favour of negotiating a bigger production allowance over leaving the bloc altogether. And there's merit to that stance. I mean, why surrender your bargaining power within the group when the very threat of leaving might help to secure a better deal?

As for what this means to the oil market, let's not be mistaken that these two countries leaving OPEC doesn't magically bring millions of additional barrels to market. It will still take much investment, infrastructure and time.

Trump's push here is mostly to try and trigger a snowball effect, particularly after the UAE's departure earlier this year. But for now, he's not going to get it his way on this one.

Circling back to the oil market, the OPEC+ meeting on 29 November this weekend will be a key risk event in seeing if the bloc can continue to keep its members' individual production ambitions aligned with its collective interest in supporting oil prices.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Reminder: Wall Street is back today but will dip buyers have the last laugh?
item.description:
It looks like dip buyers are coming back from their Thanksgiving dinner with quite the appetite. US futures are storming higher so far today, with S&P 500 futures up 1.8% and Nasdaq futures up a whopping 2.8% as tech shares look to end a bruising week on a brighter note.

After the impressive turnaround on Wednesday, there is a growing sense of optimism that dip buyers might finally be getting somewhere. However, the key question to end the week is whether they keep the party going when Wall Street returns later today?

As a reminder, US markets will only be open for an abbreviated trading session today. Both the NYSE and Nasdaq will close at 1800 GMT (1pm ET), three hours earlier than usual. Meanwhile, the bond market will close at 1900 GMT (2pm ET) before we break for the weekend.

Even with markets reopening though, I would expect liquidity conditions to remain rather patchy at best. Many market participants tend to take an extended break through the Thanksgiving weekend, so there might not necessarily be the usual crowd on Wall Street to greet dip buyers. But why should that matter?

In essence, fewer market players means that it will take less money to move prices. And that can make rallies look far more convincing than they really are, while also leaving the door open to some rather nasty and sudden reversals potentially. So, just be wary of that.

In looking to broader market sentiment today, I reckon the bigger test will be whether tech shares can build on the early gains once the cash market opens. The recovery on Wednesday showed that dip buyers were willing to step in at lower levels, but it's a different game altogether in trying to extend the buying and build back a more bullish appetite.

And when you throw in some potential month-end positioning ahead of Monday, it becomes even trickier to separate genuine buying conviction from temporary flows.

I'd certainly welcome a strong finish to the week after all the recent carnage and bloodbath in markets. But before getting too carried away, we also have to remind ourselves of the risks that are still present beyond the numbers on the screens.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Gold begins to find its feet again but are buyers out of the woods yet?
item.description:
Gold buyers have at least something to be thankful for this week. After a rather brutal month as a whole, the precious metal is finding a bit of a reprieve today as it pushes back above $3,600.

The question now though is how much should we really read into the latest bounce over the past few sessions?

Looking at the weekly chart, the $3,500 mark is proving to be a decent area for buyers to make a stand despite a brief slip below on Wednesday. And for the time being at least, buyers are also managing to nudge price back above the 50.0 Fib retracement level of the rally since 2022 - seen at around $3,608.

Now, those are some encouraging signals but the technical damage from breaking below the 100-week moving average (red line) earlier this month is still very much intact.

That being said, there is something a little more promising on the hourly chart today.

Gold has finally broken above its 100-hour moving average (red line), which has repeatedly kept buyers in check earlier this week. This is the first time in three weeks that the near-term bias is no longer siding with sellers. As such, that is giving buyers some momentum to work with in looking to the 200-hour moving average (blue line) at around $3,665 as the next key near-term hurdle. If buyers can move above that, then there is a stronger argument that the immediate selling pressure is starting to subside.

However, I still have my reservations when it comes to the latest bounce we're seeing here. Even as a gold bull myself, I wouldn't want to get too carried away considering the timing of the bounce this week.

While the broader risk mood is starting to look more upbeat again with US futures pointing higher, let's not forget the fact that we are potentially also getting caught in between month-end rebalancing flows and thinner liquidity conditions over the Thanksgiving holiday period. As such, I'm not sure I'd put too much stock in today's moves just yet.

Don't get me wrong. The technicals are definitely something one shouldn't ignore. However, I'd much rather see how gold fares when traders return to their desks next week and if there is appetite to hold any key near-term breaks today.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.
